answer:
1. The animation compares buying with renting using US history. It starts from every possible start month since January 1991 and asks whether the buyer or the renter was ahead after a set holding period. Each tile in the grid is one start month. Lit tiles mean the buyer was ahead, and dark tiles mean the renter was ahead. The sources named are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates.

2. The holding period changes. In frame 1, the 15-year view has every one of the 247 start months (100%) lit, so the buyer was ahead in all of them. Frame 2 says the weakest start month still left the buyer $79,829 ahead, in dollars of the day. Frame 3 switches to a ten-year hold. A block of tiles turns brown, which are start months where the renter was ahead after ten years. Frame 4 returns to the fifteen-year hold with the grid fully lit again. Frames 5 and 6 switch to a character, Nina, who is labeled illustrative. Her stay length is "unknown", and the rent tag stays "unchanged".

3. In this historical data, a buyer who held for 15 years came out ahead in every start month. At ten years, some start months favored the renter, so the result depended on how long the buyer stayed and when they bought. Nina's frames say the real answer depends on how long a person stays, which can't be known in advance. The "rent tag unchanged" frame seems to show rent being held fixed in the illustration.

4. The animation doesn't give direct advice. A viewer might take away that buying has done better the longer the owner stayed, and that a short or uncertain stay carries more risk. That would be a viewer's inference, not something the animation says.

5. The animation didn't state the advice in words. It showed the 15-year and ten-year results and said Nina's stay is unknown. The idea that you should only buy if you expect to stay a long time is my own conclusion. The animation also says "history, not a forecast", which cautions against treating the results as a prediction.
